blocks.text: However that may be, nothing is better known than the booming of this bird; yet for the benefit of the less learned, here are passages about it from more recent writers! Vincent, in the Doctrinale, book 16, ch. 151: The butorius is a bird so called from the sound of its voice, etc. Instead of a song it utters a terrifying cry. And it is said to be unable to do this unless it plunges its head into the water, so that the density of the element makes the voice it has formed within resound like a kind of thunder. Albertus: It utters a horrible sound like a horn, thrusting its bill into the mud of the marsh, so that its voice bursts forth in it like thunder. Yet it sits on the banks of lakes and marshes, where, putting its bill into the water, it produces such booms that it can easily be heard a mile away, an Italian mile. Belon, On Birds, book 4, chapter 4: When it comes upon the bank of a pool or marsh, it puts its bill into the water and produces so great a sound that no ox could bellow with so strained a voice. And the neighbouring places resound so that it is heard half a league away. [III, 47] Gesner: It is said to put its bill into the water and to raise a very great noise at the bottom of the water, with a strained voice like a bull's, which can be heard almost half a German mile away (that is, an hour's journey). A learned man, in a letter to Gesner describing the butorius under the name onocrotalus, writes: When it wishes to give voice, it either plunges its bill, which is long, into the water or sticks it into the bank. It does this after sunset, and often continues its booming the whole night. Hence the Italians call it trombono, from the sound of a trumpet, and tarabusa or terrabusa, because it pierces the earth with its bill and utters a horrible sound. For its German names, taken from the same source, see Gesner ^{(8)}. Thus Beza, not wrongly taking קאת kaath for the bittern, rendered the words of the Psalmist thus:
Ie suis au butor semblable Du desert inhabitable.

This surprises me all the more because he had no one to follow. For the Greeks, Jerome and Pagninus had rendered it pelican, Munster hoopoe, Arias cuckoo, Castalio onocrotalus, and in the Law ibis, and the Genevans cormorant, that is, phalacrocorax.

But, you will say, whether by the name קאת kaath you understand the heron or the pelican, why is it placed in deserts, when it is said in the Psalm, I am become like כקאת מדבר, the kaath of the desert; and in Es. XXXIV, 11. And the kaath and the hedgehog shall possess it; and in Soph. II, 14. Both the kaath and the hedgehog in its upper storeys, passages that deal with the desolation of Idumaea and Assyria? Is it right to assign to water birds, such as the pelican and the heron, a dwelling in desert and waterless places? Whoever published the Commentaries on the Psalms under the name of Jerome answers that there are two kinds of these birds, of which one lives in [col. 297] the waters, and its food is fish; and the other in the wilderness, and its food is venomous animals, that is, serpents, crocodiles and lizards. But there is no need to take refuge in this, since not every desert is waterless. In the interior of Marmarica, a region that is extremely desert, Ptolemy places the marsh of Cleartes, the marsh of Laccus and the marsh of Lycomedes. In the deserts of Arabia the Israelites came upon the waters of Marah and the springs of Elim, Exod. XV, 23. 27. Those, therefore, are mistaken who think that water birds nowhere find a suitable habitation in deserts ^{(9)}.
